subtitle: From your first print to Python 3.15

blocks.text: 1.1. What is Python?

Python is a high-level, interpreted, general-purpose programming language, created by Guido van Rossum and released in 1991. “High-level” means you write instructions close to the way you think about the problem, without worrying about memory or registers. “Interpreted” means the code is executed by a program, the interpreter, without a manual compilation step. “General-purpose” means it was not built for a niche: people use it to build websites, automations, data analyses, artificial intelligence models, games and command-line tools.

The name does not come from the snake, but from the British comedy group *Monty Python*. Even so, the snake became the community's symbol, and many puns (like the title of chapter 5 of this handbook) come from it.
A few characteristics define the language and will show up all the time:
**Dynamic and strong typing.** The type belongs to the value, not to the variable, and Python does not convert types silently: adding `'1' + 1` raises an error instead of “guessing” the result.
**Indentation is part of the syntax.** Blocks are defined by how the text is indented, not by braces. This forces all Python code to look similar, which makes it easier to read.
**Everything is an object.** Numbers, text, functions and even modules are objects with attributes and methods.
**Optional type annotations.** You can state the expected types (`idade: int`), and external tools check them. The interpreter neither requires nor checks them.
**Extensive standard library.** The basic installation already ships modules for files, dates, math, networking, compression, testing and much more.
1.2. Why learn Python in 2026?

Python has topped the popularity rankings for years and is the default language in data science, data engineering, machine learning and automation. But the most important reason for beginners is a different one: it lets you focus on the problem, not on the language.

The language has also changed a lot in the last decade. Features such as `match`/`case`, f-strings, dataclasses, type annotations and modern environment tooling (such as `uv`) have made Python more expressive and safer. This handbook teaches the current way straight away, showing the old way only when it helps you understand the new one or when you will run into it in existing code.
1.3. The language's philosophy
Python has a built-in “manifesto”: 19 aphorisms written by Tim Peters, called *The Zen of Python*. To read them, just import the `this` module:

blocks.title: Exercise 1 - The Zen of Python
blocks.code: import this

blocks.text: It is worth reading the whole list calmly. Three sentences sum up the spirit of the language well and will guide many decisions throughout the course: “beautiful is better than ugly”, “explicit is better than implicit” and “readability counts”. When there are two ways to write something, prefer the one that is easier for someone else to read, and that someone is often you, six months from now.

Open the source code of the `this` module (look for the `this.py` file in your installation). The text is “scrambled” with a simple cipher, an inside joke about the sentence “there should be one, and preferably only one, obvious way to do it”.
2.1. Implementations

“Python” is the language specification. The program that runs your code is an **implementation** of that specification. The main one, used by almost everyone, is **CPython**, written in C and maintained by the Python Software Foundation. When someone says “I installed Python”, this is what they mean.
There are other implementations for specific needs:

rows: Runs pure Python code much faster in many cases, thanks to a JIT compiler.
Python for microcontrollers, such as the ESP32 and Raspberry Pi Pico.
Python on the JVM/GraalVM, integrated with the Java ecosystem.
Python in the browser. This handbook's interactive platform uses Brython.

blocks.text: CPython itself now has variants. Since 3.13 there is a **GIL-free** build (*free-threaded*), in which several threads truly run Python code in parallel, and an experimental **JIT compiler**. In 3.14 the GIL-free build became officially supported. Both topics come back in Appendix A, in the performance and concurrency sections.
2.2. Versions and lifecycle
Python 2 reached end of life on January 1, 2020 and no longer receives even security fixes. If you come across `print "olá"` without parentheses in some tutorial, it is Python 2 code: move on.

The 3 series has a predictable schedule: **a new version every October**, each with about five years of support. The current version is **3.15**, released in October 2026, and the supported versions range from 3.11 to 3.15. This handbook uses 3.15 and states the minimum version whenever a feature is recent, with markers such as **3.12+**.
2.3. Installation

The recommended approach today is to use **uv**, a manager that installs Python versions, creates isolated environments and manages packages. It works the same on Windows, macOS and Linux and does not interfere with any Python the operating system may already have.

blocks.title: Exercise 2 - Installing uv and Python 3.15
blocks.code:
# Linux e macOS
$ curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# Windows (PowerShell)
> powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

$ uv python install 3.15     # ❶
$ uv run --python 3.15 python --version     # ❷
Python 3.15.x
callouts: Downloads and installs Python 3.15 into a folder managed by uv.
Runs that version's `python`. `uv run` is how you run anything inside the right environment.

blocks.text: If you prefer the official installer, on Windows use the **Python install manager**, which provides the `py` command (`py install 3.15` and then `py -3.15`). On macOS, the python.org installer also works well.

On many Linux distributions, the system Python is used by the operating system itself. Do not install packages into it with `sudo pip`; chapter 16 explains isolated environments, and uv already creates them for you.
Once installed, check:

blocks.code:
$ python --version
Python 3.15.2

blocks.text: The number after the second dot (the *micro*) changes with each bugfix release. Any 3.15.x will do.
3.1. What the interpreter is

The interpreter is the program that reads your code and runs it. It can be used in two ways: running a file (`python meu_programa.py`) or in **interactive mode**, also called the REPL (*Read, Eval, Print, Loop*): it reads a line, evaluates it, prints the result and goes back to waiting. The REPL is the best tool for experimenting, and we will use it a lot in this chapter and the next.
3.2. Opening interactive mode
Type `python` in the terminal (or `uv run python`, or `py` on Windows):

blocks.title: Exercise 3 - First interactive session
blocks.code:
$ python
Python 3.15.2 (main, ...) on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> 2 + 3          # ❶
5
>>> _ * 10         # ❷
50
>>> exit           # ❸
callouts: The `>>>` prompt means the interpreter is waiting for an instruction. An expression typed on its own has its result displayed automatically.
In interactive mode, `_` holds the last displayed result.
Exits the interpreter. In the current REPL, no parentheses are needed; `Ctrl+D` (Linux and macOS) or `Ctrl+Z` and Enter (Windows) also work.

blocks.text: 3.3. Features of the modern REPL
Since Python 3.13, interactive mode has been rewritten and is much more comfortable:
**Colors**: prompts, tracebacks and, since 3.14, the code itself as you type.
**Editing whole blocks**: the up arrow brings back an entire function, not one line at a time.
**F1** opens interactive help; **F2** shows the history without prompts, ready to copy; **F3** turns on paste mode, which accepts large blocks without messing up the indentation.
**Autocomplete** with Tab, colored by object type (3.15+).
Lines that open a block end with `:`, and the REPL then shows `...` until the block ends. An empty line closes the block:

blocks.code:
>>> for letra in 'abc':
...     print(letra.upper())
...
A
B
C

blocks.text: 3.4. Asking the language itself for help
Two built-in functions let you explore any object without leaving the REPL:

blocks.title: Exercise 4 - Exploring with dir and help
blocks.code:
texto = 'python'
print(type(texto))                      # ❶
print([m for m in dir(texto) if not m.startswith('_')][:8])   # ❷
help(str.title)                         # ❸
callouts: `type()` shows the object's class.
`dir()` lists attributes and methods. We filter out names starting with `_`, which are internal, and show only the first eight.
`help()` shows the documentation. In the REPL, leave the help screen with the `q` key.

blocks.text: 3.5. Reading error messages

Python's error messages have become much better in recent versions: they point exactly to where the problem is and often suggest the fix. Learning to read them is one of the most important skills in the course.

blocks.title: Exercise 5 - The interpreter as a teacher
blocks.code:
nomes = ['Ana', 'Bia']
nomes.append('Caio')
print(nome)          # ❶
callouts: Deliberate error: the variable is called `nomes`. Run it and read the last line of the message.

blocks.text: The output ends with something like `NameError: name 'nome' is not defined. Did you mean: 'nomes'?`. A *traceback* should be read **from the bottom up**: the last line gives the type and cause of the error; the lines above show the call path that led to it.

Other examples of suggestions: writing `nomes.push('Caio')` produces `AttributeError ... Did you mean '.append'?` (3.15+), and forgetting to close a parenthesis raises a `SyntaxError` that points to the open parenthesis, not to the next line, as used to happen.

sections.title: 3.4. Asking the language itself for help

blocks.text: 4.1. Standard output

The `print()` function writes to standard output (usually the terminal). It accepts several arguments, separates them with a space and ends with a line break. The `sep` and `end` parameters change that behavior.

blocks.title: Exercise 6 - Exploring print
blocks.code:
print('Olá, Python!')
print('Python', 3, 'é', True)               # ❶
print('2026', '11', '13', sep='-')          # ❷
print('Carregando', end='')                 # ❸
print('...', end=' ')
print('pronto!')
print()                                     # ❹
callouts: Arguments of different types are converted to text and separated by a space.
`sep` changes the separator.
`end` changes the line ending. With `end=''`, the next `print` continues on the same line.
With no arguments, it prints just a blank line.

blocks.text: 4.2. Variables and types
A variable is a **name** bound to an object. Assignment uses `=`, and the same name can be made to point to another object, of any type, at any time: that is what dynamic typing means.

blocks.title: Exercise 7 - Names and values
blocks.code:
saldo = 1500                     # ❶
taxa = 0.0125
cliente = 'Ana Souza'
ativo = True
nada = None                      # ❷

print(type(saldo), type(taxa), type(cliente), type(ativo), type(nada))

saldo = saldo * (1 + taxa)       # ❸
print(f'{saldo=}')               # ❹

dias_no_ano = 365
segundos_no_ano = 31_536_000     # ❺
print(dias_no_ano * 24 * 60 * 60 == segundos_no_ano)
callouts: `int` (integer). The basic types are `int`, `float`, `str`, `bool` and `NoneType`.
`None` represents the absence of a value.
The right-hand side is computed first and the result goes back to the same name.
The `=` inside the f-string shows the name and the value, great for debugging. Section 4.11 covers f-strings in detail.
The underscore separates thousands and is ignored by the interpreter.

blocks.text: Names follow the `snake_case` convention (lowercase words separated by `_`). Constants, which should not be changed, use uppercase letters: `TAXA_PADRAO = 0.0125`.

**Type annotations.** You can declare the expected type of a variable. The interpreter ignores the annotation, but editors and checkers such as `mypy` and `pyright` use it to find errors before execution:

blocks.code:
idade: int = 30
apelido: str | None = None        # str ou None (3.10+)
notas: list[float] = [8.5, 9.0]   # lista de floats (3.9+)

blocks.text: 4.3. Built-in objects
Some functions and types are always available, without `import`: these are the *builtins*. You have already used `print`, `type`, `dir` and `help`. Others that show up all the time:

rows: Size of a sequence or collection.
Convert values to the given type.
Reads a line typed by the user (always as `str`).
Sorted / reversed version of a collection.
Opens the debugger at that point in the code.

blocks.text: To see the full list: `import builtins; print(dir(builtins))`.
4.4. Type conversions
Python does not convert types on its own when the operation would be ambiguous. You convert explicitly:

blocks.title: Exercise 8 - Converting values
blocks.code:
idade_texto = '42'
print(idade_texto + '1')          # ❶
print(int(idade_texto) + 1)       # ❷
print(float('3.75') * 2)
print(str(100) + ' reais')
print(int(9.99))                  # ❸
print(round(9.99), round(2.5), round(3.5))   # ❹
print(bool(0), bool(''), bool([]), bool('0'))   # ❺
callouts: With two strings, `+` concatenates: the result is `'421'`.
Converting to `int`, `+` adds: `43`.
`int()` **truncates** the decimal part; it does not round.
`round()` uses “banker's rounding”: ties go to the nearest even number, so `round(2.5)` is `2` and `round(3.5)` is `4`.
Zero, empty text and empty collections are “falsy”. Any non-empty text is truthy, even `'0'`.

blocks.text: An operation between `str` and `int` (such as `'idade: ' + 30`) raises `TypeError`. That is strong typing in action. The fix is to convert (`str(30)`) or, better, to use an f-string (section 4.11).
4.5. Numbers
Python integers have no size limit, and `float` values follow the IEEE 754 standard, with the well-known imprecisions of that format.

blocks.title: Exercise 9 - Numeric operations
blocks.code:
print(7 / 2, 7 // 2, 7 % 2, 2 ** 10)   # ❶
print(-7 // 2)                           # ❷
print(2 ** 100)                          # ❸
print(0.1 + 0.2)                         # ❹
print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)

from decimal import Decimal
print(Decimal('0.1') + Decimal('0.2') == Decimal('0.3'))   # ❺

import math
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))     # ❻
print(math.sqrt(2), math.pi, math.floor(-2.5))
callouts: Regular division (always `float`), integer division, remainder and power.
Integer division rounds down, so with negatives the result is `-4`, not `-3`.
Integers grow as much as needed.
`0.30000000000000004`: binary cannot represent `0.1` exactly.
For money, use `Decimal`, created from text.
To compare `float` values, use a tolerance.

blocks.text: 4.6. Strings
Text values have type `str`, immutable sequences of Unicode characters. They can be written with single or double quotes, and with triple quotes for multiple lines.

blocks.title: Exercise 10 - Working with text
blocks.code:
nome = 'Programação em Python'
print(len(nome), nome[0], nome[-1])     # ❶
print(nome[:11], nome[15:], nome[::-1]) # ❷
print(nome.upper(), nome.lower())
print(nome.split())                     # ❸
print('-'.join(['2026', '11', '13']))   # ❹
print('python' in nome.lower())         # ❺

arquivo = 'relatorio_2026.csv'
print(arquivo.removesuffix('.csv'))     # ❻
print(arquivo.startswith('relat'), arquivo.endswith('.csv'))
print('  espaços  '.strip() + '|')
callouts: Indexes start at 0; negative indexes count from the end.
Slicing `[início:fim:passo]`. The end is not included; `[::-1]` reverses.
`split()` breaks the text into a list of words.
`join()` does the reverse: it joins a list using the text as the separator.
`in` checks whether a fragment is contained in the text.
`removesuffix` and `removeprefix` (3.9+) remove an exact fragment from the end or the start.

blocks.text: `strip('.csv')` does **not** remove the “.csv” suffix: it removes any of the characters `.`, `c`, `s` and `v` from both ends. For suffixes, always use `removesuffix`.
Because strings are immutable, methods like `upper()` return a **new** string; the original does not change. Trying `nome[0] = 'p'` raises `TypeError`.
4.7. Lists
The list is the most widely used collection: ordered, mutable and able to hold values of any type.

blocks.title: Exercise 11 - Lists
blocks.code:
compras = ['café', 'pão', 'leite']
compras.append('queijo')               # ❶
compras.insert(0, 'manteiga')
print(compras, len(compras))

compras.remove('pão')                  # ❷
ultimo = compras.pop()                 # ❸
print(ultimo, compras)

precos = [12.5, 3.0, 25.9, 8.75]
print(sorted(precos), max(precos), sum(precos))
precos.sort(reverse=True)              # ❹
print(precos)

matriz = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
print(matriz[1][0])                    # ❺
primeiro, *resto = precos              # ❻
print(primeiro, resto)
callouts: `append` adds at the end; `insert` at a position.
`remove` deletes the first occurrence of the value.
`pop` removes and returns the last item (or the one at the given position).
`sort()` sorts **the list itself**; `sorted()`, used earlier, returns a new one.
Lists can contain lists.
Unpacking with `*`: the first item goes to `primeiro`, the rest to `resto`.

blocks.text: 4.8. Tuples
A tuple is like an **immutable** list. Use it to group values that form a unit, such as coordinates or a record, and when you want to guarantee that nothing will be changed.

blocks.title: Exercise 12 - Tuples
blocks.code:
ponto = (10, 20)
x, y = ponto                       # ❶
print(x, y)

cor = ('azul',)                    # ❷
print(type(cor), type(('azul')))

a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a                        # ❸
print(a, b)

registro = ('Ana', 31, 'Sorocaba')
nome, idade, _ = registro          # ❹
print(f'{nome} tem {idade} anos')
callouts: Unpacking: each element goes to a variable.
A one-element tuple needs the comma. Without it, the parentheses are just grouping.
Swapping values without a helper variable: the right-hand side creates a tuple, which is unpacked.
`_` is the convention for “a value I don't care about”.

blocks.text: 4.9. Dictionaries
A dictionary (`dict`) maps **keys** to **values**. Keys must be immutable (text, numbers, tuples), and since Python 3.7 a dictionary **preserves insertion order**.

blocks.title: Exercise 13 - Dictionaries
blocks.code:
pessoa = {'nome': 'Ana', 'idade': 31}
pessoa['cidade'] = 'Sorocaba'             # ❶
print(pessoa['nome'], len(pessoa))

print(pessoa.get('email'))                # ❷
print(pessoa.get('email', 'sem e-mail'))

for chave, valor in pessoa.items():       # ❸
    print(f'{chave}: {valor}')

extra = {'idade': 32, 'cursos': ['python']}
print(pessoa | extra)                     # ❹
pessoa |= extra
print(pessoa)

del pessoa['cursos']
print('cursos' in pessoa)                 # ❺
callouts: Assigning to a new key creates the pair; to an existing key, it replaces the value.
`get` returns `None` (or the given default) if the key does not exist. By contrast, `pessoa['email']` would raise `KeyError`.
`items()` iterates over the key-value pairs, in insertion order.
`|` merges two dictionaries into a new one; the right side wins on conflict. `|=` updates in place (3.9+).
`in` checks whether a **key** exists.

blocks.text: Python 3.15 introduced `frozendict`, an immutable dictionary. It can be used as a key of another dictionary or as a set item, and it is ideal for settings that should not change: `config = frozendict(host='localhost', porta=5432)`. Any attempt to modify it raises `TypeError`.
4.10. Sets
A set (`set`) holds values **without repetition and without guaranteed order**. It is the right tool for removing duplicates and for operations such as intersection and difference.

blocks.title: Exercise 14 - Sets
blocks.code:
turma_a = {'Ana', 'Bia', 'Caio', 'Davi'}
turma_b = {'Caio', 'Davi', 'Eva'}

print(turma_a & turma_b)     # ❶
print(turma_a | turma_b)     # ❷
print(turma_a - turma_b)     # ❸
print(turma_a ^ turma_b)     # ❹

repetidos = [3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3]
print(sorted(set(repetidos)))   # ❺
print('Eva' in turma_b)         # ❻
vazio = set()                   # ❼
print(type(vazio), type({}))
callouts: Intersection: who is in both classes.
Union: everyone, without repetition.
Difference: who is in A but not in B.
Symmetric difference: who is in only one of the classes.
The classic way to remove duplicates (and `sorted` to get a predictable order).
Checking whether an item belongs to a set is very fast, even with millions of items.
`{}` creates an empty dictionary, not a set. For an empty set, use `set()`.

blocks.text: 4.11. String interpolation
Interpolating means building a text with values inside it. The modern, recommended way is **f-strings**: an `f` before the quotes and expressions inside braces.

blocks.title: Exercise 15 - f-strings
blocks.code:
produto = 'Notebook'
preco = 4599.9
quantidade = 3

print(f'{quantidade}x {produto}: R$ {preco * quantidade:.2f}')   # ❶
print(f'{produto:>12}|{produto:<12}|{produto:^12}|')             # ❷
print(f'{1234567.891:,.2f}')                                      # ❸
print(f'{0.0875:.1%}')                                            # ❹
print(f'{preco=:.1f}')                                            # ❺

itens = ['café', 'pão']
print(f'Lista: {', '.join(itens)}')                               # ❻
callouts: Any expression is valid inside the braces; after `:` comes the format (`.2f` = two decimal places).
Right, left and center alignment, with width 12.
Thousands separator.
Percentage format.
The `=` shows the expression and the value.
Since 3.12, the expression can use the same kind of quotes as the f-string.

blocks.text: You will still find two older forms in existing code: `'Olá, {}'.format(nome)`, useful when the text template comes from outside (a translation file, for example) and needs to be filled in later; and `'Olá, %s' % nome`, which today only appears in legacy code and in the `logging` module.

**Template strings (3.14+).** With `t` instead of `f`, the result is not a `str` but a `Template` object that keeps the fixed text and the values separately. This lets you process the values before joining them, for example escaping HTML in user-typed data:

blocks.code:
from html import escape from string.templatelib import Interpolation, Template def html_seguro(modelo: Template) -> str: partes = [] for parte in modelo: match parte: case str(): partes.append(parte) case Interpolation(value=valor): partes.append(escape(str(valor))) return ''.join(partes) comentario = '' print(html_seguro(t'

{comentario}

'))

blocks.title: Challenge 1 - Receipt
blocks.prompt: Given the dictionary `carrinho` (product: (quantity, unit price)), build the variable `cupom`, a `str` with one line per product in the format `produto` left-aligned in 12 positions, the quantity right-aligned in 3 positions, an `x` and the subtotal with two decimal places, right-aligned in 9 positions. The last line must be `TOTAL` aligned the same way as the products, followed by the total right-aligned in 13 positions. Lines are separated by `\n`. At the end, print the receipt.
blocks.check:
linhas = cupom.split('\n')
assert len(linhas) == 4, 'esperado 3 produtos + TOTAL'
assert linhas[0] == 'café          2x    37.80', repr(linhas[0])
assert linhas[1] == 'pão          10x     8.00', repr(linhas[1])
assert linhas[3] == 'TOTAL               88.30', repr(linhas[3])
blocks.solution:
carrinho = {'café': (2, 18.9), 'pão': (10, 0.8), 'queijo': (1, 42.5)}

linhas = []
total = 0
for produto, (qtd, unitario) in carrinho.items():
    subtotal = qtd * unitario
    total += subtotal
    linhas.append(f'{produto:<12}{qtd:>3}x{subtotal:>9.2f}')
linhas.append(f'{"TOTAL":<12}{total:>13.2f}')
cupom = '\n'.join(linhas)
print(cupom)

blocks.text: So far we have used the interactive interpreter. Now we will write programs in files, which can be run as many times as we want. Throughout the chapter, a single program will evolve through several versions: a **compound interest calculator**. Each version adds a concept.
5.1. Setting up the editor

Any text editor will do, but a code editor helps a lot. The recommendation is **VS Code** with the official Python extension and **Ruff** set up as formatter and linter: it applies the PEP 8 style guide automatically and flags common mistakes as you type. Popular alternatives: PyCharm and Zed.
Create a folder for the course. With uv, it becomes a project with one line:

blocks.code:
$ uv init curso-python && cd curso-python
$ uv run python --version

blocks.text: 5.2. First version
The compound interest formula is `montante = capital * (1 + taxa) ** periodos`.

blocks.title: Exercise 16 - Compound interest, version 1
blocks.code:
capital = 1000
taxa = 0.01          # ❶
meses = 12
montante = capital * (1 + taxa) ** meses
print('Montante:', montante)
callouts: 1% per month, written as a fraction.

blocks.text: Run it with `python juros_v1.py` (or `uv run juros_v1.py`). The result is `Montante: 1126.825030131969`: correct, but with too many decimal places.
5.3. Formatting the output

blocks.title: Exercise 17 - Compound interest, version 2
blocks.code:
capital = 1000
taxa = 0.01
meses = 12
montante = capital * (1 + taxa) ** meses
print(f'Montante: R$ {montante:,.2f}')     # ❶
print(f'Juros:    R$ {montante - capital:,.2f}')
callouts: Two decimal places and a thousands separator (section 4.11).

blocks.text: Python source files are UTF-8 by default, so accented characters work without any configuration. The `# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-` line, common in old tutorials, is no longer needed. And since 3.15, reading and writing files also uses UTF-8 by default, on any operating system.
5.4. Shebang: running as a program

On Linux and macOS, the first line of a script can state which interpreter should run it. That way, the file can be run directly (`./juros_v3.py`), after it is given execute permission (`chmod +x juros_v3.py`).

blocks.title: Exercise 18 - Compound interest, version 3
blocks.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
capital = 1000
taxa = 0.01
meses = 12
montante = capital * (1 + taxa) ** meses
print(f'Montante: R$ {montante:,.2f}')

blocks.text: `/usr/bin/env python3` looks for the `python3` active in the environment instead of a fixed path, which is why it works on any machine. On Windows the line is ignored (the `py` command knows how to read it).

Single-file scripts can even declare their own dependencies in a special comment (PEP 723). uv reads that block, prepares a temporary environment and runs it: `uv run script.py`. We will come back to this in the packages chapter.
5.5. Using the standard library
Python comes with “batteries included”: hundreds of ready-made modules. We will use `datetime` to show the date on which the investment matures.

blocks.title: Exercise 19 - Compound interest, version 4
blocks.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta     # ❶

capital = 1000
taxa = 0.01
meses = 12
montante = capital * (1 + taxa) ** meses
vencimento = date.today() + timedelta(days=30 * meses)   # ❷
print(f'Montante: R$ {montante:,.2f} em {vencimento:%d/%m/%Y}')   # ❸
callouts: Imports only the names needed from the module.
`timedelta` represents a time interval; added to a date, it produces another date. (We use 30-day months for simplicity.)
Dates accept their own formats inside the f-string.

blocks.text: 5.6. Data input
Values hard-coded in the program are not very useful. The `input()` function reads what the user types, **always as text**, so we need to convert it.

blocks.title: Exercise 20 - Compound interest, version 5
blocks.code:
capital = float(input('Capital (R$): '))          # ❶
taxa = float(input('Taxa ao mês (%): ')) / 100    # ❷
meses = int(input('Meses: '))
montante = capital * (1 + taxa) ** meses
print(f'Montante: R$ {montante:,.2f}')
callouts: `input` shows the message and waits for Enter; `float` converts the text.
The user types `1` for 1%, and the program converts it to `0.01`.

blocks.text: Try typing `mil` as the principal. The program ends with `ValueError`. Section 5.10 deals with this problem.
5.7. Modules and the name `__main__`

Every `.py` file is a **module** and can be imported by another. When imported, the module's code runs. That is a problem for our program: importing `juros_v5` would ask the user questions. The solution is to check the special variable `__name__`, which equals `'__main__'` only when the file is run directly.

blocks.title: Exercise 21 - Compound interest, version 6
blocks.code:
if __name__ == '__main__':                       # ❶
    capital = float(input('Capital (R$): '))
    taxa = float(input('Taxa ao mês (%): ')) / 100
    meses = int(input('Meses: '))
    montante = capital * (1 + taxa) ** meses
    print(f'Montante: R$ {montante:,.2f}')
callouts: Conditional `if` statement: the indented block only runs if the condition is true.

blocks.text: The block is defined by indentation. Always use **4 spaces** per level (the editor does this for you when you press Tab). Mixing spaces and tabs in the same file raises `TabError`.
5.8. Functions
Now the calculation is isolated in a **function**, which can be reused by other modules and tested separately.

blocks.title: Exercise 22 - Compound interest, version 7
blocks.code:
def montante(capital: float, taxa: float, meses: int) -> float:   # ❶
    """Calcula o montante com juros compostos."""                  # ❷
    return capital * (1 + taxa) ** meses                           # ❸


if __name__ == '__main__':
    c = float(input('Capital (R$): '))
    t = float(input('Taxa ao mês (%): ')) / 100
    m = int(input('Meses: '))
    print(f'Montante: R$ {montante(c, t, m):,.2f}')
callouts: `def` creates the function. The annotations (`: float`, `-> float`) document the expected types and the return type.
The *docstring* describes the function and appears in `help(montante)`.
`return` hands the result back to the caller.

blocks.text: Now, in another file or in the REPL, `from juros_v7 import montante` brings in the function **without** running the questions.
5.9. Command-line arguments
Terminal programs usually receive data as arguments: `python juros.py 1000 1 12`. The `sys` module gives access to them through the `sys.argv` list, whose first element is the script name.

blocks.title: Exercise 23 - Looking inside sys.argv
blocks.code:
import sys

print(sys.argv)            # ❶
print(len(sys.argv) - 1, 'argumento(s)')
callouts: Run it with `python argumentos.py 1000 1 12`: the output is `['argumentos.py', '1000', '1', '12']`. All arguments arrive as text.

blocks.text: Using `sys.argv` directly forces you to validate everything by hand: number of arguments, type conversion, usage messages. For real programs, the standard library offers the `argparse` module, which does this for you.
5.10. Final version: argparse and error handling

blocks.title: Exercise 24 - Compound interest, final version
blocks.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Calculadora de juros compostos."""
import argparse
import sys


def montante(capital: float, taxa: float, meses: int) -> float:
    """Calcula o montante com juros compostos."""
    return capital * (1 + taxa) ** meses


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:               # ❶
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument('capital', type=float, help='valor inicial em R$')     # ❷
    parser.add_argument('taxa', type=float, help='taxa ao mês, em %')
    parser.add_argument('meses', type=int, help='prazo em meses')
    parser.add_argument('--detalhe', action='store_true',
                        help='mostra a evolução mês a mês')               # ❸
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)                                         # ❹

    if args.capital <= 0 or args.meses <= 0:
        parser.error('capital e meses devem ser positivos')               # ❺

    taxa = args.taxa / 100
    if args.detalhe:
        for mes in range(1, args.meses + 1):
            print(f'mês {mes:>3}: R$ {montante(args.capital, taxa, mes):>12,.2f}')
    print(f'Montante: R$ {montante(args.capital, taxa, args.meses):,.2f}')
    return 0                                                               # ❻


if __name__ == '__main__':
    sys.exit(main())
callouts: The logic lives in `main`, which accepts an optional list of arguments. This lets you test it without a terminal: `main(['1000', '1', '12'])`.
Each positional argument has a type and help text. If the user types `mil`, argparse shows the error and exits with code 2, without any `if` of ours.
An optional “on/off” argument.
Parses the arguments. Try `python juros.py --help`: the help is generated automatically.
Business-rule validations use `parser.error`, which keeps the same message pattern.
Exit code 0 means success; `sys.exit` returns it to the operating system.

blocks.text: Compare with version 5: the program now validates its input, explains how it should be used, can be imported and can be tested. This is the format we will use from now on for terminal programs.

When you need to convert user input without argparse, the idiomatic way in Python is to **try and handle the error** (`try: valor = int(texto) except ValueError: ...`) instead of checking beforehand with methods like `isnumeric()`. That method accepts characters such as `'²'`, which `int()` rejects, so the up-front check guarantees nothing. The principle has a name: *it is easier to ask for forgiveness than permission* (EAFP). Exception handling is the subject of chapter 11.

Use `choices` in argparse to accept only `c` or `f`. The function must return `0`. Remember: `F = C * 9/5 + 32`.

def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    ...


main(['100', 'c'])
blocks.check:

saida = io.StringIO()
with contextlib.redirect_stdout(saida):
    r1 = main(['100', 'c'])
    r2 = main(['32', 'f'])
linhas = saida.getvalue().strip().split('\n')
assert r1 == 0 and r2 == 0, 'main deve devolver 0'

import argparse


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description='Converte temperaturas.')
    parser.add_argument('valor', type=float)
    parser.add_argument('escala', choices=['c', 'f'])
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    if args.escala == 'c':
        print(f'{args.valor:.1f} C = {args.valor * 9 / 5 + 32:.1f} F')
    else:
        print(f'{args.valor:.1f} F = {(args.valor - 32) * 5 / 9:.1f} C')
    return 0


main(['100', 'c'])

sections.title: 5.10. Final version: argparse and error handling

blocks.text: Programs rarely follow a straight line: they repeat, choose and stop. In this chapter we look at loops and the tools that make them short and readable. Decisions with `if` and `match` get their own chapter, 11.
6.1. The while loop
`while` repeats a block **as long as** a condition is true. It is the right choice when you do not know in advance how many repetitions will be needed.

blocks.title: Exercise 25 - Countdown
blocks.code:
contador = 5
while contador > 0:          # ❶
    print(contador, end=' ')
    contador -= 1            # ❷
print('Fogo!')
callouts: The condition is evaluated before each repetition.
`-=` is the short form of `contador = contador - 1`. Without this line, the loop would never end.

blocks.text: 6.2. The walrus operator
A very common pattern is “compute a value, test it and use it”. The `:=` operator (nicknamed the *walrus*, because of its shape) assigns **inside** an expression and avoids repeating the computation.

blocks.title: Exercise 26 - Reading until the empty line
blocks.code:
respostas = iter(['banana', 'maçã', 'uva', ''])   # ❶

frutas = []
while (fruta := next(respostas)) != '':          # ❷
    frutas.append(fruta.title())
print(frutas)

numeros = [3, 18, 7, 42, 11]
if (n := len(numeros)) > 4:                      # ❸
    print(f'Lista grande: {n} itens')
callouts: `iter` turns the list into a source of values consumed one by one with `next()`. Here it simulates a user typing.
Reads, stores in `fruta` and compares, all in the loop condition.
It also works in `if`. The parentheses are required in most contexts.

blocks.text: Use `:=` when it removes a real repetition. For ordinary assignments, `=` is still clearer.
6.3. Unpacking
We have already seen that `a, b = 1, 2` distributes values across names. The feature is more powerful than it looks:

blocks.title: Exercise 27 - Unpacking everything
blocks.code:
primeiro, *meio, ultimo = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]    # ❶
print(primeiro, meio, ultimo)

(x1, y1), (x2, y2) = [(0, 0), (3, 4)]             # ❷
print(((x2 - x1) ** 2 + (y2 - y1) ** 2) ** 0.5)

def estatisticas(valores):
    return min(valores), max(valores), sum(valores) / len(valores)   # ❸

menor, maior, media = estatisticas([4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42])
print(f'{menor=} {maior=} {media=:.1f}')
callouts: The name with `*` collects “the rest” into a list.
Nested structures are unpacked in one go.
A function that returns several values actually returns a tuple.

blocks.text: 6.4. The for loop
`for` goes through the items of any **iterable**: lists, text, dictionaries, files, `range`. It is the most used loop in Python, and you almost never need to manage an index by hand.

blocks.title: Exercise 28 - Iterating over collections
blocks.code:
notas = {'Ana': 9.5, 'Bia': 7.0, 'Caio': 8.25}

for nome in notas:                              # ❶
    print(nome, end=' ')
print()

for posicao, (nome, nota) in enumerate(notas.items(), start=1):   # ❷
    print(f'{posicao}º {nome:<5} {nota:5.2f}')

nomes = ['Ana', 'Bia', 'Caio']
idades = [31, 27, 45]
for nome, idade in zip(nomes, idades, strict=True):   # ❸
    print(f'{nome} tem {idade} anos')
callouts: Iterating over a dictionary directly iterates over its **keys**.
`enumerate` yields the position along with the item. Combined with unpacking, it avoids any `[i]`.
`zip` walks through several sequences in parallel. With `strict=True` (3.10+), an error is raised if they have different lengths, instead of silently truncating.

blocks.text: 6.5. range, sum and friends

blocks.title: Exercise 29 - Sums and sequences
blocks.code:
print(list(range(5)), list(range(2, 10, 3)), list(range(5, 0, -1)))   # ❶

total = 0
for n in range(1, 101):
    total += n
print(total, sum(range(1, 101)))                                     # ❷

pares = sum(n for n in range(1, 101) if n % 2 == 0)                  # ❸
print(pares)
print(any(n > 99 for n in range(100)), all(n >= 0 for n in range(100)))   # ❹
callouts: `range(fim)`, `range(início, fim)` and `range(início, fim, passo)`. The end is never included.
The manual loop and the `sum` function reach the same result; prefer the latter.
A *generator expression* (chapter 8) inside `sum`.
`any` and `all` answer “any?” and “all?” without explicit loops.

blocks.text: 6.6. break, continue and else
`break` stops the loop; `continue` skips to the next iteration. A little-known detail: loops accept `else`, which runs **only if the loop finishes without `break`**.

blocks.title: Exercise 30 - Looking for a prime number
callouts: Found a divisor: not prime, exit the loop.
The `for` loop's `else` only runs if no `break` happened, that is, no divisor was found.
Skips even numbers without running the rest of the block.

blocks.text: 6.7. Iteration tools
The `itertools` module solves common loop patterns in one line:

blocks.title: Exercise 31 - itertools in everyday use
blocks.code:
from itertools import accumulate, chain, groupby, pairwise

vendas = [120, 80, 200, 150]
print(list(accumulate(vendas)))                       # ❶
print([b - a for a, b in pairwise(vendas)])           # ❷
print(list(chain([1, 2], (3, 4), 'ab')))              # ❸

palavras = sorted(['ana', 'bia', 'ari', 'beto', 'caio'])
for letra, grupo in groupby(palavras, key=lambda p: p[0]):   # ❹
    print(letra, list(grupo))
callouts: Running totals.
`pairwise` (3.10+) yields neighboring pairs, ideal for differences between periods.
Chains several iterables as if they were one.
Groups **consecutive** items with the same key; that is why the list is sorted first.

blocks.text: For processing data in batches, 3.12 introduced `itertools.batched`: `batched(range(7), 3)` produces `(0, 1, 2)`, `(3, 4, 5)` and `(6,)`.
6.8. Recursion

A **recursive** function calls itself, reducing the problem until it reaches a trivial case. Python limits recursion depth (usually 1000 calls) and does not optimize tail calls, so recursion is best suited to naturally recursive problems, such as tree structures.

blocks.title: Exercise 32 - Summing a nested structure
blocks.code:
def soma_profunda(item) -> int:
    match item:                                    # ❶
        case int():
            return item
        case list() | tuple():
            return sum(soma_profunda(x) for x in item)   # ❷
        case _:
            return 0


dados = [1, [2, 3], [4, [5, [6]]], 'ignorado']
print(soma_profunda(dados))
callouts: `match` picks the case by the value's type (details in chapter 11).
The recursive step: the sum of a list is the sum of the sums of its items.

blocks.text: 6.9. Conditional expression
To choose between two values, Python has a one-line expression: `valor_se_verdadeiro if condição else valor_se_falso`.

blocks.title: Exercise 33 - Choosing values
blocks.code:
for saldo in (250.0, -40.0, 0.0):
    situacao = 'positivo' if saldo > 0 else 'negativo' if saldo < 0 else 'zerado'   # ❶
    print(f'{saldo:>8.2f} {situacao}')

nome = ''
print(f'Olá, {nome or "visitante"}!')     # ❷
callouts: Chaining two expressions works, but more than that hurts readability: use `if`/`elif`.
`or` returns the first truthy value, a common shortcut for default values.

blocks.title: Challenge 4 - FizzBuzz with statistics
blocks.prompt: Write the function `fizzbuzz(n)` that returns a **list** with the values from 1 to `n`, replacing multiples of 3 with `'Fizz'`, multiples of 5 with `'Buzz'` and multiples of both with `'FizzBuzz'` (the others remain `int`). Then write `contagem(n)`, which returns a dictionary with how many times each word appeared, for example `{'Fizz': 27, 'Buzz': 14, 'FizzBuzz': 6}` for `n=100`.
blocks.check:
assert fizzbuzz(15) == [1, 2, 'Fizz', 4, 'Buzz', 'Fizz', 7, 8, 'Fizz', 'Buzz', 11, 'Fizz', 13, 14, 'FizzBuzz'], fizzbuzz(15)
assert contagem(100) == {'Fizz': 27, 'Buzz': 14, 'FizzBuzz': 6}, contagem(100)
blocks.solution:
def fizzbuzz(n: int) -> list:
    resultado = []
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        match (i % 3, i % 5):
            case (0, 0):
                resultado.append('FizzBuzz')
            case (0, _):
                resultado.append('Fizz')
            case (_, 0):
                resultado.append('Buzz')
            case _:
                resultado.append(i)
    return resultado


def contagem(n: int) -> dict:
    total = {}
    for item in fizzbuzz(n):
        if isinstance(item, str):
            total[item] = total.get(item, 0) + 1
    return total


print(fizzbuzz(15))
print(contagem(100))

blocks.text: Files are the simplest way for a program to keep data between runs. This chapter covers reading and writing text, CSV and JSON, and using `pathlib` to handle paths.

The interactive lab's engine runs in the browser and has no access to your disk. That is why the runnable examples in this chapter use `io.StringIO`, an “in-memory file” that behaves exactly like an open file. The examples with real files are marked for local execution.
7.1. Opening files safely
The `open()` function returns a file object. Every open file must be closed, even when an error happens along the way. The `with` block guarantees this automatically.

blocks.title: Exercise 34 - Writing and reading a file
blocks.code:
with open('notas.txt', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as arquivo:   # ❶
    arquivo.write('Ana;9.5\n')
    arquivo.write('Bia;7.0\n')
    print('Caio;8.25', file=arquivo)                       # ❷

with open('notas.txt', encoding='utf-8') as arquivo:       # ❸
    for linha in arquivo:                                  # ❹
        nome, nota = linha.strip().split(';')
        print(f'{nome:<6}{float(nota):>6.2f}')
callouts: Mode `'w'` creates or overwrites; `'a'` appends to the end; `'r'` (the default) reads. Always declare the `encoding`.
`print` accepts a file as its destination.
When leaving the `with` block, the file is closed, even in case of error.
Iterating over the file reads one line at a time, without loading everything into memory.

blocks.text: since 3.15, `open()` without `encoding` uses UTF-8 on any system. Before that, Windows used the regional encoding, and accented characters written on one system showed up garbled on another. Even so, declare `encoding='utf-8'` so the code behaves the same on earlier versions.
The same idea, in the lab, with an in-memory file:

blocks.title: Exercise 35 - In-memory file
blocks.code:
import io

arquivo = io.StringIO('Ana;9.5\nBia;7.0\nCaio;8.25\n')    # ❶
media = 0
linhas = 0
for linha in arquivo:
    nome, nota = linha.strip().split(';')
    media += float(nota)
    linhas += 1
print(f'Média da turma: {media / linhas:.2f}')
callouts: `StringIO` takes the initial content and offers the same methods as a text file.

blocks.text: 7.2. Paths with pathlib
The `pathlib` module represents paths as objects, with clear operations that are independent of the operating system (the `/` slash builds paths on any system):

blocks.title: Exercise 36 - Working with paths
blocks.code:
from pathlib import Path

base = Path('dados')
base.mkdir(exist_ok=True)                           # ❶
relatorio = base / '2026' / 'vendas.csv'            # ❷
relatorio.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
relatorio.write_text('mes,valor\njan,100\n', encoding='utf-8')   # ❸

print(relatorio.name, relatorio.stem, relatorio.suffix)          # ❹
print(relatorio.read_text(encoding='utf-8'))
for csv in base.rglob('*.csv'):                     # ❺
    print('encontrado:', csv)
callouts: Creates the folder if it does not exist.
The `/` operator joins path parts.
Shortcuts for small files: `write_text` and `read_text`.
Full name, name without extension, and extension.
Recursive search by pattern. `Path.walk()` (3.12+) walks the folder tree.

blocks.text: 7.3. CSV
CSV is the most common data exchange format. The `csv` module correctly handles quotes, commas inside fields and line breaks.

blocks.title: Exercise 37 - Reading and writing CSV
blocks.code:
import csv
import io

entrada = io.StringIO('nome,cidade,salario\nAna,"São Paulo, SP",8500\nBia,Sorocaba,7200\n')
leitor = csv.DictReader(entrada)                      # ❶
pessoas = [linha for linha in leitor]
print(pessoas[0])

saida = io.StringIO()
escritor = csv.writer(saida, delimiter=';')           # ❷
escritor.writerow(['nome', 'salario_anual'])
for p in pessoas:
    escritor.writerow([p['nome'], int(p['salario']) * 13])
print(saida.getvalue())
callouts: `DictReader` uses the first line as the header and yields each line as a dictionary. Notice that the comma inside `"São Paulo, SP"` was respected.
`delimiter` changes the separator, common in Brazilian spreadsheets, which use `;`.

blocks.text: With real files, open CSVs with `newline=''`: `open('dados.csv', encoding='utf-8', newline='')`. Without it, fields with line breaks are read incorrectly and, on Windows, extra blank lines appear when writing. Files from government agencies often come in Latin-1: in that case, use `encoding='latin-1'`.
7.4. JSON
JSON is the standard format for APIs and configuration files. The `json` module converts between it and Python types (`dict`, `list`, `str`, numbers, `bool` and `None`).

blocks.title: Exercise 38 - Converting to and from JSON
blocks.code:
import json

pedido = {'id': 1042, 'cliente': 'Ana', 'itens': [{'produto': 'café', 'qtd': 2}], 'pago': True}
texto = json.dumps(pedido, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)    # ❶
print(texto)

de_volta = json.loads(texto)                                # ❷
print(de_volta['itens'][0]['produto'], de_volta == pedido)
callouts: `dumps` produces the JSON text. `ensure_ascii=False` keeps accented characters readable; `indent` formats it.
`loads` does the reverse. For files, use `json.dump(obj, arquivo)` and `json.load(arquivo)`.

blocks.title: Challenge 5 - Sales report by region

Compute total sales **per region** and store in the variable `relatorio` a dictionary `{região: total}` with the regions in alphabetical order and the totals as `float`. Then produce in `saida` the JSON of that dictionary (with `ensure_ascii=False`) and print it.

import io
import json

dados = io.StringIO('regiao,vendedor,valor\nSul,Ana,1200.50\nNorte,Bia,800\nSul,Caio,300\nSudeste,Davi,2500.25\nNorte,Eva,200\n')

relatorio = {}
saida = ''

blocks.check:
assert relatorio == {'Norte': 1000.0, 'Sudeste': 2500.25, 'Sul': 1500.5}, relatorio
assert list(relatorio) == ['Norte', 'Sudeste', 'Sul'], 'as regiões devem estar em ordem alfabética'

blocks.solution:
import csv
import io
import json

dados = io.StringIO('regiao,vendedor,valor\nSul,Ana,1200.50\nNorte,Bia,800\nSul,Caio,300\nSudeste,Davi,2500.25\nNorte,Eva,200\n')

print(saida)

blocks.text: *Comprehensions* are a compact way to create collections from other collections, combining loop, filter and transformation in a single expression. Used in moderation, they make code shorter **and** more readable.
8.1. List comprehension

blocks.title: Exercise 39 - From loop to comprehension
blocks.code:
precos = [19.9, 5.5, 120.0, 42.0, 8.75]

com_desconto = []
for p in precos:                                       # ❶
    if p > 10:
        com_desconto.append(round(p * 0.9, 2))
print(com_desconto)

com_desconto = [round(p * 0.9, 2) for p in precos if p > 10]   # ❷
print(com_desconto)

rotulos = ['caro' if p > 50 else 'barato' for p in precos]    # ❸
print(rotulos)
callouts: The loop version: create an empty list, iterate, filter, append.
The same logic in one line: `[expressão for item in iterável if condição]`.
A conditional expression in the **expression** part transforms every item; the `if` at the end **filters**.

blocks.text: 8.2. Dict and set comprehensions

blocks.title: Exercise 40 - Dictionaries and sets by comprehension
blocks.code:
produtos = ['café', 'pão', 'leite', 'queijo']
tamanhos = {p: len(p) for p in produtos}                  # ❶
print(tamanhos)

estoque = {'café': 0, 'pão': 30, 'leite': 0, 'queijo': 4}
faltando = {p for p, qtd in estoque.items() if qtd == 0}  # ❷
print(sorted(faltando))

invertido = {v: k for k, v in {'a': 1, 'b': 2}.items()}  # ❸
print(invertido)
callouts: Keys and values separated by `:`.
With braces and a single value, the result is a `set`.
A classic trick: swapping keys and values.

blocks.text: 8.3. Generator expressions

Swap the square brackets for parentheses and the comprehension becomes a **generator expression**: instead of building the whole list in memory, it produces one item at a time, on demand. When summing millions of values, the difference in memory is huge.

blocks.title: Exercise 41 - Generating on demand
blocks.code:
import sys

quadrados_lista = [n * n for n in range(100_000)]
quadrados_gen = (n * n for n in range(100_000))          # ❶
print(type(quadrados_gen).__name__)
print(sum(quadrados_lista) == sum(quadrados_gen))        # ❷
print(sum(quadrados_gen))                                # ❸
callouts: Parentheses: nothing is computed yet.
Values are computed as `sum` asks for them.
A generator can only be iterated **once**: the second sum gives `0`.

blocks.text: 8.4. Nested comprehensions and filters with :=

blocks.title: Exercise 42 - Matrices and filters
blocks.code:
matriz = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
transposta = [[linha[i] for linha in matriz] for i in range(3)]   # ❶
print(transposta)
plana = [x for linha in matriz for x in linha]                    # ❷
print(plana)

textos = ['10', 'abc', '7', '', '42']
numeros = [n for t in textos if (n := int(t) if t.isdigit() else None) is not None]   # ❸
print(numeros)
callouts: One comprehension inside another. Read it from the outside in.
Two `for` clauses in the same comprehension, in the **same order** as the equivalent loops.
`:=` computes once and reuses the value in the filter.

blocks.text: in 3.15, comprehensions accept unpacking: `[*linha for linha in matriz]` flattens the matrix, and `{**d for d in lista_de_dicts}` merges several dictionaries. Both forms replace the “double for” from item 2.
If the comprehension does not fit comfortably on one or two lines, or needs more than one `if`, go back to a regular loop. Readability counts.

blocks.text: Functional programming is a style that treats functions as values, avoids changing data and prefers to compose small transformations. Python is not a pure functional language, but it offers the main tools, and mixing the two styles is common and healthy.
9.1. Functions are objects
In Python, functions are **first-class objects**: they can be stored in variables and data structures, passed as arguments and returned by other functions.

blocks.title: Exercise 43 - Functions as values
blocks.code:
def dobro(x): return x * 2
def quadrado(x): return x ** 2

operacoes = {'dobro': dobro, 'quadrado': quadrado, 'oposto': lambda x: -x}   # ❶
for nome, funcao in operacoes.items():
    print(f'{nome:>8}(7) = {funcao(7)}')

calcula = quadrado                       # ❷
print(calcula(9), calcula is quadrado, calcula.__name__)
callouts: A dictionary of functions: an elegant alternative to long chains of `if`.
Assigning does not call the function: it just creates another name for the same object.

blocks.text: 9.2. Higher-order functions
A **higher-order** function takes or returns another function. `map`, `filter` and `sorted(key=...)` are built-in examples.

blocks.title: Exercise 44 - map, filter and key
blocks.code:
from functools import reduce
from operator import itemgetter, mul

produtos = [('café', 18.9), ('pão', 0.8), ('queijo', 42.5), ('leite', 5.49)]

print(sorted(produtos, key=itemgetter(1)))                 # ❶
print(list(map(lambda p: p[0].upper(), produtos)))         # ❷
print(list(filter(lambda p: p[1] < 10, produtos)))
print(reduce(mul, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))                        # ❸

def aplicar_n_vezes(funcao, n, valor):                     # ❹
    for _ in range(n):
        valor = funcao(valor)
    return valor

print(aplicar_n_vezes(lambda x: x * 2, 10, 1))
callouts: `key` takes a function that extracts the sort criterion. `itemgetter(1)` is equivalent to `lambda p: p[1]`.
`map` and `filter` return iterators; `list` materializes them. A comprehension is often more readable.
`reduce` combines the items two at a time until a single value is left.
Our own higher-order function.

blocks.text: 9.3. Closures
A **closure** is a function that “remembers” the variables of the scope in which it was created, even after that scope has ended.

blocks.title: Exercise 45 - Function factory
blocks.code:
def criar_desconto(percentual: float):
    def aplicar(preco: float) -> float:          # ❶
        return round(preco * (1 - percentual / 100), 2)
    return aplicar                               # ❷

black_friday = criar_desconto(30)
funcionario = criar_desconto(15)
print(black_friday(200), funcionario(200))       # ❸

def contador():
    total = 0
    def incrementar():
        nonlocal total                           # ❹
        total += 1
        return total
    return incrementar

c = contador()
print(c(), c(), c())
callouts: The inner function uses `percentual`, which belongs to the outer function.
Returns the function without calling it.
Each closure keeps its own `percentual`.
To **change** a variable from the outer scope, you must declare it `nonlocal`.

blocks.text: 9.4. Lambdas

`lambda` creates an anonymous function made of a single expression. It is useful for short arguments, such as the `key` of `sorted`. If you need a name, more than one line or documentation, use `def`.

blocks.title: Exercise 46 - Sorting with lambdas
blocks.code:
alunos = [{'nome': 'Bia', 'nota': 8.0}, {'nome': 'Ana', 'nota': 9.5}, {'nome': 'Caio', 'nota': 8.0}]
por_nota = sorted(alunos, key=lambda a: (-a['nota'], a['nome']))   # ❶
print([a['nome'] for a in por_nota])
callouts: The key can be a tuple: grade in descending order (thanks to the negative sign) and, on ties, name in alphabetical order.

blocks.text: 9.5. Immutability

Data that does not change is easier to understand and share. Python offers immutable versions of the main collections: `tuple` (list), `frozenset` (set) and, since 3.15, `frozendict` (dictionary). For your own objects, `@dataclass(frozen=True)` (chapter 13).

blocks.title: Exercise 47 - Transforming without changing
blocks.code:
original = (3, 1, 2)
ordenada = tuple(sorted(original))           # ❶
print(original, ordenada)

def adicionar(colecao: tuple, item) -> tuple:
    return (*colecao, item)                  # ❷

base = ('a', 'b')
nova = adicionar(base, 'c')
print(base, nova)

from types import MappingProxyType
config = MappingProxyType({'debug': False})  # ❸
try:
    config['debug'] = True
except TypeError as e:
    print('não pode:', e)
callouts: Instead of changing a value, create a new one.
Unpacking to build a new tuple.
A read-only “view” of a dictionary, available in versions before 3.15.

blocks.text: 9.6. Lazy evaluation with generators
A function with `yield` becomes a **generator**: on each `next()`, it runs until the next `yield`, hands over the value and pauses. This lets you work with huge or even infinite sequences.

blocks.title: Exercise 48 - Infinite sequences
callouts: An infinite loop is not a problem: nothing is computed until someone asks.
Generators can consume other generators, forming a *pipeline*.
`islice` takes only the first items.
The two generators work together, one item at a time.

blocks.text: 9.7. functools: cache and partial

blocks.title: Exercise 49 - Memoizing results
callouts: `@cache` stores the result for each combination of arguments. Without it, this function would make millions of repeated calls.
`partial` fixes some arguments of a function, creating another one.

blocks.text: 9.8. Limits of the functional style in Python

Some tools common in functional languages do not exist in Python: there is no tail-call optimization (deep recursion hits the limit) and no native function-composition operator. On the other hand, since 3.10 the language has **structural pattern matching** with `match`/`case`, the subject of chapter 11. To dispatch a function based on the argument's type, there is also `functools.singledispatch`.

blocks.title: Challenge 7 - Function pipeline
blocks.prompt: Write `compor(*funcoes)`, which returns a function that applies the given functions **from left to right**: `compor(f, g, h)(x)` must equal `h(g(f(x)))`. With no functions, it must return the value itself. Use `functools.reduce`.

def compor(*funcoes):
    ...


limpar = compor(str.strip, str.lower, lambda s: s.replace(' ', '-'))
print(limpar('  Python Moderno  '))

blocks.text: 10.1. Kinds of parameters
A function's parameters can be filled by position or by name, can have default values and can even require one of the two forms.

blocks.title: Exercise 50 - Positional, keyword and defaults
callouts: Everything before `/` is **positional-only**; everything after `*` is **keyword-only** (3.8+).
Passing `True` by position is forbidden. This prevents ambiguous calls like `transferir(a, b, 150, True)`, where nobody knows what `True` means.

blocks.text: 10.2. *args and **kwargs

blocks.title: Exercise 51 - Variable number of arguments
blocks.code:
def registrar(evento: str, *valores, **detalhes):        # ❶
    print(f'[{evento}] valores={valores} detalhes={detalhes}')

registrar('login')
registrar('compra', 19.9, 5.5, cliente='Ana', cupom='BEMVINDO')

def media(*numeros: float) -> float:
    return sum(numeros) / len(numeros) if numeros else 0.0

notas = [8.0, 9.5, 7.25]
print(media(*notas))                                    # ❷
opcoes = {'sep': ' | ', 'end': '!\n'}
print('a', 'b', 'c', **opcoes)                          # ❸
callouts: `*valores` receives the extra positional arguments as a tuple; `**detalhes`, the extra keyword arguments as a dictionary.
In the **call**, `*` spreads a sequence into positional arguments...
... and `**` spreads a dictionary into keyword arguments.

blocks.text: 10.3. The mutable default value trap
A parameter's default value is created **only once**, when the function is defined. If it is mutable (list, dictionary), all calls share the same object.

blocks.title: Exercise 52 - The classic bug
blocks.code:
def adicionar_errado(item, lista=[]):          # ❶
    lista.append(item)
    return lista

print(adicionar_errado('a'), adicionar_errado('b'))   # ❷

def adicionar(item, lista=None):               # ❸
    if lista is None:
        lista = []
    lista.append(item)
    return lista

print(adicionar('a'), adicionar('b'))
callouts: The default list is created only once.
Result: `['a', 'b'] ['a', 'b']`. The second call “inherited” the item from the first.
The standard fix: `None` as a “not provided” signal and the list created inside the function. Linters like Ruff flag this mistake automatically.

blocks.text: when `None` is a valid value and you need to tell “not provided” apart, 3.15 offers the `sentinel` built-in: `FALTANDO = sentinel('FALTANDO')` and `def atualizar(email=FALTANDO)`. It has a readable name and is understood by type checkers, unlike the old `FALTANDO = object()` trick.
10.4. Type annotations in functions
Annotating parameters and return values documents the function's contract and lets tools find errors before execution. Since 3.12, generic functions and type aliases have their own syntax:

Since 3.14, annotations are only evaluated when someone inspects them, so you can reference classes defined further down in the file, without quotes. Remember: the interpreter does **not** check types. That is the job of `mypy`, `pyright` and editors.
10.5. Callable objects
Any object with a `__call__` method can be called like a function. It is an alternative to closures when you need to keep state in an organized way.

blocks.title: Exercise 53 - A class that behaves like a function
callouts: Defines what happens when we write `limite(v)`.

blocks.text: 10.6. Decorators

A **decorator** is a function that takes a function and returns another, usually “wrapping” the original with extra behavior. The `@decorator` syntax above `def` is just a shortcut for `funcao = decorator(funcao)`.

blocks.title: Exercise 54 - Timing and logging calls
callouts: `wraps` copies the name, docstring and other metadata from the original function to the wrapper.
`*args, **kwargs` lets you decorate functions with any signature.
A decorator **with parameters** is a function that returns a decorator: three levels of functions.
Thanks to `wraps`, the decorated function is still called `soma`.

blocks.title: Challenge 8 - Retry decorator
blocks.prompt: Write the parameterized decorator `tentar(vezes)`. It must call the decorated function and, if it raises `ConnectionError`, try again, up to a total of `vezes` attempts. If all of them fail, re-raise the last exception. Other exceptions must not be retried. Preserve the function's name with `wraps`.

blocks.text: 11.1. if, elif and else

The `if` statement runs a block when the condition is true; `elif` tests alternatives in sequence; `else` covers whatever is left. Python allows **chained comparisons**, which make value ranges very readable.

blocks.title: Exercise 55 - Value ranges
callouts: `18.5 <= imc < 25` is equivalent to `18.5 <= imc and imc < 25`. Continuous ranges with `<` and `<=` leave no “gaps” between one case and the next, which easily happens when you use `in range(...)` with integers.

blocks.text: 11.2. Pattern matching with match/case

For many years Python had no statement like the `switch` of other languages, and the workaround was to use dictionaries or chains of `elif`. Since 3.10 there is something much more powerful: **structural pattern matching**. It compares the **shape** of a value and, at the same time, extracts parts of it.

blocks.title: Exercise 56 - Values and alternatives
blocks.code:
def tipo_de_dia(dia: int) -> str:
    match dia:
        case 1 | 7:                          # ❶
            return 'fim de semana'
        case 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6:
            return 'dia útil'
        case _:                              # ❷
            return 'dia inválido'


print([tipo_de_dia(d) for d in range(0, 9)])

def faixa_etaria(idade: int) -> str:
    match idade:
        case int() if idade < 0:             # ❸
            return 'inválida'
        case int() if idade < 18:
            return 'menor de idade'
        case int() if idade < 60:
            return 'adulto'
        case int():
            return 'idoso'
        case _:
            raise TypeError('idade deve ser um inteiro')


print([faixa_etaria(i) for i in (-1, 10, 18, 59, 60)])
callouts: `|` joins several alternatives in the same case.
`_` matches anything: it is the “default case”.
`int()` checks the type; the `if` after the pattern is a **guard**, an extra condition.

blocks.text: The power of `match` shows up with structures: lists, tuples, dictionaries and objects.

blocks.title: Exercise 57 - Matching structures
blocks.code:
def executar(comando: str) -> str:
    match comando.split():
        case ['sair']:
            return 'encerrando'
        case ['abrir', arquivo]:                         # ❶
            return f'abrindo {arquivo}'
        case ['copiar', origem, destino]:
            return f'copiando {origem} para {destino}'
        case ['apagar', *arquivos] if arquivos:          # ❷
            return f'apagando {len(arquivos)} arquivo(s)'
        case _:
            return f'comando desconhecido: {comando!r}'


for c in ['sair', 'abrir notas.txt', 'copiar a.txt b.txt', 'apagar x y z', 'apagar', 'voar']:
    print(executar(c))


def descrever(evento: dict) -> str:
    match evento:
        case {'tipo': 'pagamento', 'valor': int() | float() as valor} if valor >= 1000:   # ❸
            return f'pagamento alto: {valor}'
        case {'tipo': 'pagamento', 'valor': valor}:
            return f'pagamento: {valor}'
        case {'tipo': 'erro', 'codigo': 404 | 410}:
            return 'recurso não encontrado'
        case {'tipo': tipo}:
            return f'evento {tipo} ignorado'


print(descrever({'tipo': 'pagamento', 'valor': 2500}))
print(descrever({'tipo': 'pagamento', 'valor': 30, 'moeda': 'BRL'}))    # ❹
print(descrever({'tipo': 'erro', 'codigo': 404}))
print(descrever({'tipo': 'login'}))
callouts: A name inside the pattern **captures** the value at that position.
`*arquivos` captures the rest of the list; the guard requires at least one.
Dictionary patterns check the given keys; `as` names the matched value.
Extra keys in the dictionary do not get in the way of the match.

blocks.text: A bare name in a `case` **always** matches and captures the value, overwriting the variable. To compare against a constant, use a literal, a dotted name (`case Cor.AZUL:`) or a guard.
11.3. Loops with else and early exit
Revisiting chapter 6 with a search example: a loop's `else` is the idiomatic way to handle the “I looked and didn't find it” case.

blocks.title: Exercise 58 - Searching with for/else

blocks.text: 11.4. Exception handling
Runtime errors raise **exceptions**. Without handling, the program ends; with `try`/`except`, you decide what to do.

blocks.title: Exercise 59 - try, except, else and finally
callouts: Keep in the `try` only the code that can fail with the exceptions you handle.
`as` gives access to the exception object.
`else` runs only if **no** exception occurred.
`finally` runs **always**, with or without an error. Use it to release resources.

blocks.text: Several types can be handled in the same block. Since 3.14 the parentheses are optional when there is no `as`: `except ValueError, TypeError:`. In earlier versions, write `except (ValueError, TypeError):`.

Avoid generic `except:` or `except Exception:` clauses that just ignore the error: they hide bugs. And since 3.14, `return`, `break` or `continue` inside `finally` trigger a warning, because they silently swallow any exception in flight.
11.5. Raising exceptions and chaining causes

blocks.title: Exercise 60 - Custom exceptions and from
callouts: Custom exceptions inherit from `Exception` and can hold data useful to whoever handles them.
`raise` raises the exception.
`from erro` records the original cause. The traceback shows both, which makes debugging much easier.

blocks.text: 11.6. Exception notes and groups

Two additions from 3.11 help in larger programs. `add_note()` adds context to an exception without replacing it with another. `ExceptionGroup` raises **several** exceptions at once, for example when validating all the fields of a form, and `except*` handles each type in the group separately.

blocks.title: Exercise 61 - Validating everything at once
callouts: The group carries all the failures, not just the first one.
Each `except*` receives the subset of the group with that type. Both blocks run.
The note appears in the traceback, below the message.

blocks.title: Challenge 9 - Order router
blocks.prompt: Write `processar(pedido)` using `match`. The order is a dictionary. Rules: if `tipo` is `'pix'` and there is a `valor`, return `'pix:<valor>'`; if `tipo` is `'cartao'` with `valor` and `parcelas` greater than 1, return `'cartao:<valor>/<parcelas>x'`; `'cartao'` with `valor` and no `parcelas` (or with 1) returns `'cartao:<valor>'`. Any other shape must raise `ValueError`.
blocks.solution:
def processar(pedido: dict) -> str:
    match pedido:
        case {'tipo': 'pix', 'valor': valor}:
            return f'pix:{valor}'
        case {'tipo': 'cartao', 'valor': valor, 'parcelas': int() as p} if p > 1:
            return f'cartao:{valor}/{p}x'
        case {'tipo': 'cartao', 'valor': valor}:
            return f'cartao:{valor}'
        case _:
            raise ValueError(f'pedido inválido: {pedido!r}')


print(processar({'tipo': 'pix', 'valor': 50}))

blocks.text: 12.1. Modules
Every `.py` file is a module. `import` runs the module once, on the first import, and caches the result; later imports reuse the same object.

blocks.title: Exercise 62 - Ways to import
blocks.code:
import math                                  # ❶
from statistics import mean, median          # ❷
from datetime import datetime as dt          # ❸
import random as rnd

print(math.ceil(4.1), mean([1, 2, 3, 10]), median([1, 2, 3, 10]))
print(dt(2026, 11, 13).strftime('%d/%m/%Y'))
rnd.seed(42)                                 # ❹
print(rnd.randint(1, 6), rnd.choice(['pedra', 'papel', 'tesoura']))
callouts: Imports the module; access uses the `math.` prefix.
Imports specific names into the current scope.
`as` creates an alias.
Fixing the seed makes the “random” numbers reproducible, which is useful in tests.

blocks.text: Avoid `from modulo import *`. It brings unknown names into your code, can overwrite variables and makes it hard to find out where each name came from.
12.2. Packages

A **package** is a folder of modules. The `__init__.py` file marks the folder as a regular package and runs on the first import; it is common to use it to expose the package's public interface. A typical structure, with code in `src/` and tests kept separate:

blocks.code:
loja/
├── pyproject.toml
├── src/
│   └── loja/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       ├── __main__.py        # permite: python -m loja
│       ├── precos.py
│       └── pagamentos/
│           ├── __init__.py
│           └── pix.py
└── tests/
    └── test_precos.py

blocks.title: Exercise 63 - A package and its modules
blocks.code:
# src/loja/precos.py
def com_desconto(valor: float, percentual: float) -> float:
    return round(valor * (1 - percentual / 100), 2)

# src/loja/pagamentos/pix.py
from ..precos import com_desconto                  # ❶

def valor_pix(valor: float) -> float:
    return com_desconto(valor, 5)

# src/loja/__init__.py
from .precos import com_desconto                   # ❷
from .pagamentos.pix import valor_pix

__all__ = ['com_desconto', 'valor_pix']             # ❸

# src/loja/__main__.py
from loja import valor_pix
print(f'R$ 100,00 no pix: R$ {valor_pix(100):.2f}')   # ❹
callouts: **Relative** import: `.` is the current package and `..` the package above.
`__init__.py` re-exports the important names, so users can just write `from loja import com_desconto`.
`__all__` declares the public interface.
With `__main__.py`, the package becomes executable: `python -m loja`.

blocks.text: The `src/` layout avoids a subtle problem: without it, tests may import the local folder instead of the installed package and pass by mistake. Chapter 15 shows how to install the package in development mode.
12.3. Lazy imports (3.15)

Large programs, especially command-line tools, lose startup time importing libraries that may not even be used in that run. 3.15 introduced the `lazy` keyword, which defers loading until the name is first used:

`lazy` is only allowed at module level (not inside functions, classes or `try`). If the module does not exist, the error shows up on first use, and the traceback also shows the import line. To stay compatible with earlier versions, there is the alternative `__lazy_modules__ = ['json']` at the top of the file: 3.15 honors it, and older versions simply ignore it.

blocks.title: Challenge 10 - Plugin registry
blocks.prompt: Simulate a plugin system with a **dictionary of modules**. Write the decorator `plugin(nome)`, which registers the decorated function in the `REGISTRO` dictionary under that name and returns the function unchanged. Then write `executar(nome, *args)`, which calls the registered plugin; if the name does not exist, raise `LookupError` with a message that includes the available plugins in alphabetical order.

blocks.text: 13.1. Classes and instances
A **class** describes a kind of object: what data it holds (attributes) and what it can do (methods). Each object created from it is an **instance**.

blocks.title: Exercise 64 - A first class
blocks.code:
class Conta:
    def __init__(self, titular: str, saldo: float = 0.0):    # ❶
        self.titular = titular                                # ❷
        self.saldo = saldo

    def depositar(self, valor: float) -> None:                # ❸
        if valor <= 0:
            raise ValueError('depósito deve ser positivo')
        self.saldo += valor

    def __str__(self) -> str:                                 # ❹
        return f'{self.titular}: R$ {self.saldo:,.2f}'

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f'Conta({self.titular!r}, {self.saldo!r})'


ana = Conta('Ana', 100)
ana.depositar(50)
print(ana)
print(repr(ana))
print([ana])                                                  # ❺
callouts: `__init__` initializes the newly created instance.
`self` is the instance itself; attributes are created by assigning to `self.algo`.
Methods receive `self` as their first parameter, but in the call it is passed automatically.
`__str__` defines the “friendly” text used by `print`; `__repr__`, the technical representation, which ideally looks like the code that recreates the object.
Collections display their items with `repr`.

blocks.text: 13.2. Dataclasses
Classes that exist mainly to hold data require a lot of repetitive code: `__init__`, `__repr__`, `__eq__`. The `@dataclass` decorator generates all of it from the annotations.

blocks.title: Exercise 65 - Tasks with dataclass
blocks.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from datetime import date


@dataclass
class Tarefa:
    descricao: str
    prazo: date | None = None                     # ❶
    feita: bool = False
    etiquetas: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)   # ❷

    def concluir(self) -> None:
        self.feita = True

    def atrasada(self, hoje: date) -> bool:       # ❸
        return not self.feita and self.prazo is not None and self.prazo < hoje


t1 = Tarefa('Pagar boleto', date(2026, 11, 10), etiquetas=['casa'])
t2 = Tarefa('Pagar boleto', date(2026, 11, 10), etiquetas=['casa'])
print(t1)
print(t1 == t2)                                   # ❹
print(t1.atrasada(date(2026, 11, 13)))


@dataclass(frozen=True, order=True)               # ❺
class Versao:
    maior: int
    menor: int

print(sorted([Versao(3, 15), Versao(3, 9), Versao(2, 7)]))
callouts: Fields with a default value come after the required ones.
For mutable defaults, `field(default_factory=list)` creates a new list for each instance (remember chapter 10.3).
Taking “today” as a parameter, instead of calling `date.today()` inside, makes the method predictable and easy to test.
The generated `__eq__` compares field by field.
`frozen=True` makes instances immutable; `order=True` generates `<`, `>` and allows sorting. Other useful options: `slots=True` (less memory) and `kw_only=True`.

blocks.text: 13.3. Making objects iterable

Objects integrate with the language by implementing **special methods** (the *dunder methods*, from *double underscore*). With `__iter__` and `__len__`, an object works in `for`, `list()` and `len()`.

blocks.title: Exercise 66 - A project that contains tasks
callouts: Delegating to the internal list's iterator is enough.
Overloading the `+=` operator. It must return `self`.
`__contains__` defines the behavior of the `in` operator.

blocks.text: 13.4. Duck typing and Protocol

In Python, what matters is what the object **can do**, not which class it inherits from: “if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck”. `typing.Protocol` formalizes this for type checkers, without requiring inheritance.

blocks.title: Exercise 67 - Interchangeable notifiers
callouts: The protocol only describes the expected method.
`Console` and `Memoria` do not inherit from `Notificador`, but both are accepted: having `enviar` is enough.

blocks.text: 13.5. Domain exceptions and encapsulation

By convention, names starting with `_` are internal: they work normally, but signal “do not use from outside”. Names with `__` (two underscores, no trailing underscores) are renamed internally to avoid clashes in subclasses, but this is not security, just organization.

blocks.title: Exercise 68 - Finding tasks
callouts: The `_` marks an internal attribute.
`next` with a generator expression takes the first result without building a whole list.
`from None` hides the `StopIteration`, which is an implementation detail of no interest to the caller.
