blocks.text: 14.1. Class and instance members
Attributes defined in the class body belong to the **class** and are shared by all instances. Attributes created on `self` belong to each **instance**.

blocks.title: Exercise 69 - Counting instances
blocks.code:
class Pedido:
    taxa_entrega = 7.5            # ❶
    _proximo_numero = 1

    def __init__(self, cliente: str):
        self.cliente = cliente
        self.numero = Pedido._proximo_numero       # ❷
        Pedido._proximo_numero += 1


p1, p2 = Pedido('Ana'), Pedido('Bia')
print(p1.numero, p2.numero, p1.taxa_entrega)
Pedido.taxa_entrega = 9.9                          # ❸
print(p1.taxa_entrega, p2.taxa_entrega)
p1.taxa_entrega = 0                                # ❹
print(p1.taxa_entrega, p2.taxa_entrega, Pedido.taxa_entrega)
callouts: Class attribute.
To change the shared value, access it through the class.
Changing it on the class affects every instance that does not have its own value.
Assigning through the instance creates an **instance** attribute, which shadows the class one.

blocks.text: 14.2. Class and static methods

blocks.title: Exercise 70 - Alternative constructors
callouts: `@classmethod` receives the class (`cls`) instead of the instance. It is the standard pattern for alternative constructors and also works in subclasses.
`@staticmethod` receives neither class nor instance: it is a regular function that lives in the class namespace.
Comparing tuples compares item by item; `True` counts as 1 and `False` as 0 in subtraction.

blocks.text: 14.3. Properties
Properties let you expose a method as if it were an attribute, with validation on write, without changing how it is used.

blocks.title: Exercise 71 - Validating with @property
callouts: Even in `__init__`, the assignment goes through the *setter* and is validated.
The *setter* intercepts `p.preco = valor`.
A read-only property, computed on each access.
`cached_property` computes once and stores the result on the instance.

blocks.text: 14.4. Abstract classes
An abstract class defines an interface that subclasses **are required** to implement; it cannot be instantiated itself.

blocks.title: Exercise 72 - Geometric shapes
callouts: Abstract classes can have concrete methods that use the abstract ones.
`@override` (3.12+) declares that the method overrides one from the parent class. If someone renames the method in the parent class, the type checker warns you.
Trying to instantiate the abstract class raises `TypeError`.

blocks.text: When subclasses do not need to inherit any behavior, only follow a contract, prefer `Protocol` (section 13.4): it is more flexible and does not require inheritance.
14.5. Multiple inheritance, mixins and MRO

A class can inherit from several others. To decide which method to use when names repeat, Python follows the **method resolution order** (MRO). A common and safe use of multiple inheritance is **mixins**: small classes that add a capability.

blocks.title: Exercise 73 - Mixins
callouts: A mixin can use methods from another mixin.
`super()` calls the **next** class in the MRO, not necessarily the direct parent class. That is why cooperative mixins always pass the arguments along.
The class's full MRO.

blocks.text: 14.6. Enumerations
Related constants (statuses, colors, levels) become safer and more readable with `enum`. `StrEnum` (3.11+) makes each member also behave as text.

blocks.title: Exercise 74 - Order status
blocks.code:
from enum import Enum, StrEnum, auto


class Status(StrEnum):
    PENDENTE = auto()                      # ❶
    PAGO = auto()
    ENVIADO = auto()
    CANCELADO = auto()


def proxima_acao(status: Status) -> str:
    match status:
        case Status.PENDENTE:              # ❷
            return 'aguardar pagamento'
        case Status.PAGO:
            return 'separar e enviar'
        case Status.ENVIADO | Status.CANCELADO:
            return 'nada a fazer'


print([str(s) for s in Status])
print(proxima_acao(Status('pago')))       # ❸
print(Status.ENVIADO == 'enviado')
callouts: In a `StrEnum`, `auto()` uses the lowercase name as the value.
Dotted names in a `case` compare against the constant instead of capturing.
Converts text (from a database or a JSON file, for example) into the corresponding member.

blocks.text: 14.7. The iteration protocol

Underneath every `for` is the **iteration protocol**: `iter(obj)` returns an iterator, and `next(iterador)` yields the next item until it raises `StopIteration`. Implementing the protocol by hand helps you understand the mechanism; in practice, a generator (section 9.6) does the same in fewer lines.

blocks.title: Exercise 75 - Manual iterator and generator
blocks.code:
class Contagem:
    def __init__(self, inicio: int, fim: int):
        self.atual, self.fim = inicio, fim

    def __iter__(self):
        return self

    def __next__(self) -> int:               # ❶
        if self.atual > self.fim:
            raise StopIteration
        valor = self.atual
        self.atual += 1
        return valor


def contagem(inicio: int, fim: int):         # ❷
    yield from range(inicio, fim + 1)


print(list(Contagem(1, 5)), list(contagem(1, 5)))
it = iter([10, 20])
print(next(it), next(it), next(it, 'acabou'))   # ❸
callouts: Each call yields a value or signals the end.
The same behavior with a generator; `yield from` delegates to another iterable.
`next` accepts a default value for when the iterator is exhausted.

blocks.text: 15.1. PyPI and pip

**PyPI** (pypi.org) is the official Python package repository, with hundreds of thousands of libraries. **pip** is the installer that ships with Python. Always call it through the interpreter, to be sure which Python is receiving the package:

blocks.title: Exercise 76 - Essential pip commands
blocks.code:
$ python -m pip install httpx              # ❶
$ python -m pip install "httpx>=0.27,<1"   # ❷
$ python -m pip show httpx                 # ❸
$ python -m pip list --outdated
$ python -m pip uninstall httpx
$ python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt  # ❹
$ python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
callouts: Installs the latest version and its dependencies.
Version specifiers limit the accepted range.
Shows the version, dependencies and install location.
Records the exact versions of everything installed.

blocks.text: To search for packages, use the pypi.org website: the old `pip search` command has not worked since 2020.

On many Linux distributions, running `pip install` on the system Python ends with the `externally-managed-environment` error (PEP 668). This is deliberate: installing packages there can break system tools. Do not force it with `--break-system-packages`. Use a virtual environment (chapter 16) or uv, and for command-line tools, `uv tool install` or `pipx`.
15.2. The pyproject.toml file
The current standard for describing a Python project is `pyproject.toml`. It declares the name, version, minimum Python version, direct dependencies, terminal commands and tool configuration.

blocks.title: Exercise 77 - A complete pyproject.toml
blocks.code:
[project]
name = "loja"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "Cálculos de preços e pagamentos"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = ["httpx>=0.27"]               # ❶

[project.scripts]
loja = "loja.__main__:main"                  # ❷

[dependency-groups]
dev = ["pytest>=8", "ruff>=0.6", "mypy>=1.11"]   # ❸

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100                            # ❹
callouts: Only the **direct** dependencies, with version ranges.
Creates the `loja` terminal command when the package is installed.
Dependencies used only during development.
Tools read their own configuration from the same file.

blocks.text: The `tomllib` module (3.11+) reads TOML files in the standard library: `tomllib.load(open('pyproject.toml', 'rb'))`.
15.3. Managing projects with uv

**uv** brings together in one tool what used to require pip, venv, pip-tools and pyenv: it installs Python versions, creates the environment, resolves dependencies and keeps a *lockfile* with the exact versions of everything.

blocks.title: Exercise 78 - A project's lifecycle
blocks.code:
$ uv init --package loja && cd loja     # ❶
$ uv add httpx                          # ❷
$ uv add --dev pytest ruff
$ uv run python -m loja                 # ❸
$ uv run pytest
$ uv lock --upgrade && uv sync          # ❹
$ uv build                              # ❺
$ uv tool install ruff                  # ❻
callouts: Creates `pyproject.toml`, the `src/` layout, `.python-version` and a git repository.
Adds to `pyproject.toml`, resolves and updates `uv.lock`.
Runs inside the project environment, creating it the first time.
Updates the locked versions and syncs the environment.
Builds the distribution files (wheel and sdist) in `dist/`.
Installs an isolated command-line tool, available from any folder.

blocks.text: 16.1. Why isolate

Different projects need different versions of the same libraries. If you install everything into the same Python, sooner or later one project breaks another. A **virtual environment** is a folder with its own Python and that project's packages, isolated from the rest of the system.
16.2. venv
The `venv` module ships with Python and creates virtual environments:

blocks.title: Exercise 79 - Creating and using a venv
blocks.code:
$ python -m venv .venv                     # ❶

$ source .venv/bin/activate                # ❷ Linux e macOS
> .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1               #    Windows (PowerShell)
> .venv\Scripts\activate.bat               #    Windows (cmd)

(.venv) $ python -m pip install httpx      # ❸
(.venv) $ python -c "import sys; print(sys.prefix)"
(.venv) $ deactivate                       # ❹
callouts: Creates the environment in the `.venv` folder. Since 3.13, it comes with its own `.gitignore`, so it does not end up in the repository.
Activating adjusts the terminal's `PATH` to use the environment's Python. The prompt then shows its name.
Installs now go into the environment, not the system.
Goes back to the system Python.

blocks.text: 16.3. Environments with uv

With uv, you rarely create or activate environments by hand: `uv run` and `uv sync` keep a `.venv` in the project folder, in sync with `uv.lock`. Anyone who clones the repository reproduces **exactly** the same environment with a single `uv sync`. If you prefer the traditional workflow, `uv venv` creates a regular environment, compatible with everything we saw in the previous section.
Single-file scripts can declare their own dependencies (PEP 723), with no project or manual environment:

blocks.title: Exercise 80 - Script with embedded dependencies
blocks.code:

# requires-python = ">=3.12"
# dependencies = ["httpx"]
# ///
import httpx

resposta = httpx.get('https://api.github.com', timeout=10)

blocks.text: When run with `uv run cotacao.py` (or directly, thanks to the shebang), uv reads the `# /// script` block, prepares a temporary environment with `httpx` and runs the script.
17.1. The DB-API

Python defines a common interface for relational databases, the **DB-API** (PEP 249). That is why the same code pattern works for SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and others: connect, get a cursor, run commands with parameters, read results and commit or roll back the transaction.

We will use **SQLite**, which already ships with Python (the `sqlite3` module): the database is a single file, with no server to install. At the end of the chapter, section 17.6 shows what changes for a server such as PostgreSQL or MySQL.
The interactive lab's engine does not have the `sqlite3` module. The examples in this chapter must be run on your local Python. They all run on any supported version, without installing anything.
17.2. Creating tables

blocks.title: Exercise 81 - Address book schema
blocks.code:
import sqlite3
from contextlib import closing

ESQUEMA = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS grupos (
    id        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    nome      TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS contatos (
    id        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    nome      TEXT NOT NULL,
    telefone  TEXT NOT NULL,
    grupo_id  INTEGER REFERENCES grupos(id)
);
"""

with closing(sqlite3.connect('agenda.db')) as conexao:      # ❶
    conexao.executescript(ESQUEMA)                         # ❷
    tabelas = conexao.execute(
        "SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table'"
    ).fetchall()
    print(tabelas)
callouts: `connect` opens (or creates) the database file. `closing` guarantees the connection will be closed.
`executescript` runs several commands at once. It is safe here because the text is fixed.

blocks.text: 17.3. Inserting with parameters

blocks.title: Exercise 82 - Safe inserts
blocks.code:
import sqlite3
from contextlib import closing

contatos = [('Ana', '15 99999-0001', 'Família'), ('Bia', '15 99999-0002', 'Trabalho'),
            ('Caio', '15 99999-0003', 'Família')]

with closing(sqlite3.connect('agenda.db')) as conexao:
    with conexao:                                                   # ❶
        for nome, telefone, grupo in contatos:
            conexao.execute('INSERT OR IGNORE INTO grupos (nome) VALUES (?)', (grupo,))   # ❷
            grupo_id = conexao.execute('SELECT id FROM grupos WHERE nome = ?', (grupo,)).fetchone()[0]
            conexao.execute(
                'INSERT INTO contatos (nome, telefone, grupo_id) VALUES (:nome, :tel, :grupo)',   # ❸
                {'nome': nome, 'tel': telefone, 'grupo': grupo_id},
            )
    print(conexao.execute('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM contatos').fetchone()[0], 'contatos')
callouts: `with conexao:` opens a **transaction**: it commits if everything goes well and rolls back if there is an error. Note: it does not close the connection; that is why `closing` wraps it.
`?` marks a positional parameter. The values go in a tuple, **separate** from the SQL.
You can also use named parameters, with a dictionary.

blocks.text: Never build SQL with f-strings or concatenation from external data: `f"SELECT * FROM contatos WHERE nome = '{nome}'"` allows **SQL injection**, in which a text like `' OR 1=1 --` changes the query. Parameters solve this, because the database always treats the value as data, never as code.
17.4. Querying

blocks.title: Exercise 83 - Queries, JOIN and pagination
blocks.code:
import sqlite3
from contextlib import closing

with closing(sqlite3.connect('agenda.db')) as conexao:
    conexao.row_factory = sqlite3.Row                 # ❶
    sql = """
        SELECT c.nome, c.telefone, g.nome AS grupo
        FROM contatos c LEFT JOIN grupos g ON g.id = c.grupo_id
        WHERE c.nome LIKE ?
        ORDER BY c.nome
        LIMIT ? OFFSET ?
    """
    for linha in conexao.execute(sql, ('%a%', 10, 0)):   # ❷
        print(f"{linha['nome']:<6} {linha['telefone']}  [{linha['grupo']}]")

    por_grupo = conexao.execute(
        'SELECT g.nome, COUNT(*) FROM contatos c JOIN grupos g ON g.id = c.grupo_id GROUP BY g.nome'
    ).fetchall()
    print(dict(por_grupo))                            # ❸
callouts: With `sqlite3.Row`, each row can be accessed by column name.
The cursor is iterable: rows arrive one by one. `LIMIT` and `OFFSET` paginate the result.
A list of pairs turns directly into a dictionary.

blocks.text: 17.5. Updating and deleting

blocks.title: Exercise 84 - Changes and affected row counts
blocks.code:
import sqlite3
from contextlib import closing

with closing(sqlite3.connect('agenda.db')) as conexao:
    with conexao:
        cur = conexao.execute('UPDATE contatos SET telefone = ? WHERE nome = ?', ('15 98888-0001', 'Ana'))
        print('atualizados:', cur.rowcount)              # ❶
        cur = conexao.execute('DELETE FROM contatos WHERE nome = ?', ('Inexistente',))
        print('excluídos:', cur.rowcount)                # ❷
    try:
        with conexao:
            conexao.execute('INSERT INTO contatos (nome, telefone) VALUES (?, ?)', ('Davi', None))
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError as erro:               # ❸
        print('rejeitado:', erro)
callouts: `rowcount` reports how many rows the command affected.
Zero rows is not an error for the database: if it is an error for your business rule, check `rowcount`.
Constraint violations (`NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE`) raise `IntegrityError`, and the transaction is rolled back. All the module's exceptions inherit from `sqlite3.Error`.

blocks.text: 3.12 introduced the `python -m sqlite3 agenda.db` shell for interactive queries, which in 3.15 gained colors and autocompletion of tables and columns. For dates, store ISO text (`date.isoformat()`) and convert on read with `date.fromisoformat()`: the `sqlite3` automatic date converters have been deprecated since 3.12.
17.6. Server databases
For PostgreSQL or MySQL, the code is practically the same; only the package and the connection change. Credentials must never live in the code: read them from environment variables.

Password taken from the environment, never written in the file.
Each library has its own parameter placeholder: `%s` in psycopg and the MySQL connector, `?` in SQLite. The rule is the same: never format SQL with the data.

A.1. Fibonacci: four implementations
The same problem solved in four ways, from the didactic to the idiomatic. Compare clarity and performance.

blocks.title: Exercise 86 - Fibonacci four ways
blocks.code:
from functools import cache
from itertools import islice


def fib_recursivo(n: int) -> int:                 # ❶
    return n if n < 2 else fib_recursivo(n - 1) + fib_recursivo(n - 2)


@cache
def fib_cache(n: int) -> int:                     # ❷
    return n if n < 2 else fib_cache(n - 1) + fib_cache(n - 2)


def fib_iterativo(n: int) -> int:                 # ❸
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return a


def fib_gerador():                                # ❹
    a, b = 0, 1
    while True:
        yield a
        a, b = b, a + b


print(fib_recursivo(20), fib_cache(90), fib_iterativo(90))
print(list(islice(fib_gerador(), 10)))
callouts: Straight from the mathematical definition, but exponential: `fib_recursivo(35)` already takes seconds.
With `@cache`, each value is computed only once.
Iterative: constant memory and no recursion. Usually the best choice.
Generator: produces the whole sequence on demand.

Do not optimize in the dark: measure. The `timeit` module compares small snippets; the profiler shows where a whole program spends its time.

blocks.text: A.3. A report generator that ties it all together
An example that combines several chapters: dataclass, in-memory CSV, `match`, comprehensions, `Decimal` and f-strings.

blocks.title: Exercise 88 - Financial report
blocks.code:
import csv
import io
from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal

CSV = """data,categoria,descricao,valor
2026-11-01,receita,salário,8500.00
2026-11-03,moradia,aluguel,-2200.00
2026-11-05,mercado,compras do mês,-950.40
2026-11-12,mercado,feira,-120.35
2026-11-15,lazer,cinema,-64.00
2026-11-20,receita,freela,1200.00
"""


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class Lancamento:
    data: date
    categoria: str
    descricao: str
    valor: Decimal


def ler(texto: str) -> list[Lancamento]:
    return [Lancamento(date.fromisoformat(l['data']), l['categoria'], l['descricao'], Decimal(l['valor']))
            for l in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(texto))]


def resumo(lancamentos: list[Lancamento]) -> dict[str, Decimal]:
    totais: defaultdict[str, Decimal] = defaultdict(Decimal)
    for l in lancamentos:
        match l:
            case Lancamento(categoria='receita', valor=v):     # ❶
                totais['receitas'] += v
            case Lancamento(categoria=cat, valor=v) if v < 0:
                totais[cat] += -v
    return dict(totais)


lancamentos = ler(CSV)
totais = resumo(lancamentos)
despesas = {k: v for k, v in totais.items() if k != 'receitas'}
saldo = totais['receitas'] - sum(despesas.values())

print(f"{'Receitas':<12}{totais['receitas']:>12,.2f}")
for categoria, valor in sorted(despesas.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True):
    barra = '█' * int(valor / totais['receitas'] * 40)                  # ❷
    print(f'{categoria:<12}{valor:>12,.2f}  {barra}')

blocks.text: A.4. Concurrency: threads, processes and asyncio

When a program spends most of its time **waiting** (network, disk, database), you can do several waits at the same time. Python offers three models: **threads** (`concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor`), good for I/O waits; **processes** (`ProcessPoolExecutor`), for heavy computation across several cores; and **asyncio**, in which a single thread switches between many tasks that explicitly declare where they wait (`await`).

blocks.title: Exercise 89 - Several waits at once with asyncio
blocks.code:
import asyncio
import time


async def baixar(nome: str, segundos: float) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(segundos)                        # ❶
    if nome == 'falha':
        raise ConnectionError(f'{nome}: servidor fora do ar')
    return f'{nome} ({segundos}s)'


async def main() -> None:
    inicio = time.perf_counter()
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as grupo:             # ❷
        tarefas = [grupo.create_task(baixar(n, s)) for n, s in [('a', 1), ('b', 1.5), ('c', 0.5)]]
    print([t.result() for t in tarefas], f'em {time.perf_counter() - inicio:.1f}s')   # ❸

    try:
        async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as grupo:
            grupo.create_task(baixar('d', 1))
            grupo.create_task(baixar('falha', 0.2))
    except* ConnectionError as erros:                    # ❹
        print('falhou:', [str(e) for e in erros.exceptions])


asyncio.run(main())
callouts: `await` marks the point where the task waits and frees the thread for the others.
`TaskGroup` (3.11+) starts the tasks together and only leaves the block when all of them finish.
Three downloads of 1s, 1.5s and 0.5s take about 1.5s in total, not 3s.
If a task fails, the group cancels the others and raises an `ExceptionGroup` (chapter 11.6).

blocks.text: For CPU-heavy computation, the historical limit was the GIL, which prevents threads from running Python code in parallel. Since 3.14, the **GIL-free** build of CPython (`python3.15t`) is officially supported: in it, a `ThreadPoolExecutor` truly uses all cores. Libraries with C extensions need to declare compatibility, so test before adopting it in production.
